lesson_title: Pancakes, Currency and a Rugby Pass: Chemistry Exam Essentials
hook_text: 3 cups of flour, 4 eggs, recipe says 1 cup + 2 eggs per batch. Most people count the flour. The exam counts the eggs.
clip_script: The recipe: one cup of flour and two eggs make eight pancakes. Your shelf: three cups of flour and four eggs. Instinct says the flour is plenty — three batches' worth. But run the demand check: three cups of flour demand six eggs, and the shelf holds four. The eggs run out first: the EGGS are the limiting ingredient, the flour is in excess, and the kitchen makes exactly two batches — sixteen pancakes — with a cup of flour left on the shelf, useless without partners. That demand-versus-supply check is the entire limiting-reagent method.
visual_style: A kitchen counter with flour and eggs stacked as bar charts; the demand check drawn as arrows from flour to the eggs it needs, snapping short at four; the leftover flour cup greying out while sixteen pancakes stack up; the scene morphing into a balanced equation with moles replacing cups and eggs.
mood: Kitchen game-show energy — a feared exam topic revealed as breakfast arithmetic.
pacing: Quick shelf reveal, the wrong instinct dangled, the demand check as the twist, pancake payoff and the chemistry morph.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision lesson and cross every stoichiometry bridge without a wobble.
